title: The Raise That Made Him Poorer
description: When his annual compensation jumps to thirty-four lakhs, Gurgaon operations director Bhaskar Sen upgrades to a luxury high-rise on Golf Course Extension Road—only to discover in a 2:00 AM spreadsheet that every salary increase has merely built a more expensive cage.
excerpt: The increment letter arrived as an encrypted PDF on a Friday in April, protected by a password consisting of the first four letters of his mother's maiden name and his year of birth.
author: Noble John Steeven
coverImageAlt: A lone laptop screen showing an illuminated Excel spreadsheet in a dark high-rise apartment living room at night, with the sprawling neon lights of Gurgaon visible through floor-to-ceiling glass windows

storySections.chapterTitle: I. The Letter with the New Number
storySections.heading: I. The Letter with the New Number
storySections.body:
The increment letter arrived as an encrypted PDF on a Friday in April, protected by a password consisting of the first four letters of his mother's maiden name and his year of birth.

Bhaskar Sen unlocked it while sitting in his cubicle on the ninth floor of a glass tower in Cyber City.

He was thirty-six. He had worked for seven years as a supply chain lead for a quick-commerce platform whose electric delivery scooters swarmed through Delhi's residential colonies like blue beetles. He was responsible for fourteen dark stores between DLF Phase 1 and Sector 82, tracking grocery delivery times down to four-hundred-millisecond dispatch windows.

He scrolled past the boiler-plate paragraphs about organizational resilience and core competencies to the bold tabular section on page two:

*Fixed Annual Base:* **₹28,50,000**  
*Performance Retainer:* **₹6,00,000**  
*Total Annual Cost to Company:* **₹34,50,000**  

Bhaskar stared at the figures for three minutes without blinking.

Thirty-four lakhs and fifty thousand rupees.

In Durgapur, where his father had spent thirty-four years working as a junior mechanical supervisor in the state water irrigation division, the elder Sen's final basic pension was twenty-six thousand four hundred rupees a month. Bhaskar was now earning more in sixty days than his father had earned in an entire year of maintaining canal sluice gates.

He closed the PDF. He walked to the water dispenser, poured a paper cone of lukewarm water, and looked out through the double-glazed acoustic glass.

Below him, the eight-lane concrete strip of the Delhi-Gurgaon Expressway stretched toward the horizon, shimmering under the white heat of the April sun. A stream of silver luxury sedans, container trucks, and office cabs moved along the tarmac with the relentless, unpausing velocity of an industrial assembly line.

Bhaskar felt a sharp, intoxicating rush of triumph.

He had arrived. He had escaped the humid, decaying industrial melancholy of the Durgapur steel townships: the damp lime-washed quarters with iron water filters, the single Bajaj Chetak scooter his father washed with a rag every Sunday morning, the perpetual anxiety over whether the monthly coal ration would last until the twenty-eighth.

He reached into his pocket, pulled out his phone, and dialed his wife Ruchira.

'It came through,' he said, his voice trembling slightly. 'Thirty-four point five.'

Ruchira was silent for three seconds. In the background, he could hear the click of keyboards from the educational publishing office in Okhla where she worked as a senior editor.

'Thirty-four?' she whispered.

'Thirty-four point five,' Bhaskar repeated.

'Bhaskar,' she said, her breath catching. 'We can finally leave Sector 56.'

storySections.chapterTitle: II. The Architecture of the Upgrade
storySections.heading: II. The Architecture of the Upgrade
storySections.body:
The upgrade began as an act of hygiene, then rapidly metastasized into an administrative necessity.

Their old flat in Sector 56 was twelve hundred square feet of yellowing terrazzo tiles, situated on the second floor of a four-story cooperative housing society built in 1998. The water pump broke down every three months; the balcony looked into an open transformer yard; and the parking was an unpaved mud lot where neighbors had fistfights over unassigned slots.

By June, they had signed an eleven-month lease on a twenty-four-hundred-square-foot apartment on the eighteenth floor of *The Pinnacle Crest*, a newly completed high-rise development on Golf Course Extension Road.

The complex was designed to simulate a Mediterranean resort in the middle of Haryana's semi-arid scrubland.

It had seven-tier electronic security with automated RFID vehicle recognition barriers. It had three swimming pools, four indoor squash courts, an air-conditioned squash lounge, a cigar bar, and an artificial waterfall that circulated eighty thousand liters of treated groundwater through a landscaped rockery twenty-four hours a day.

The rent was eighty-eight thousand rupees a month.

The society maintenance charge—covering the landscaping, the waterfall, the gym instructors from Ukraine, and the six armed security guards at the perimeter gates—was fourteen thousand five hundred rupees.

Then came the furniture.

The old teak dining table that Bhaskar's parents had given them as a wedding gift—sturdy, dark, slightly scratched at the legs—looked grotesque against the polished white Italian marble of the new living room. It looked like an old bullock cart parked in a sterile hospital laboratory.

'We can't put this here, Bhaskar,' Ruchira said, standing in the middle of the empty, echoing sixty-foot salon. 'It looks ridiculous.'

They spent two weekends at the luxury furniture showrooms on Mehrauli-Gurgaon Road.

They bought an eight-seater dining table with a smoked glass top and brushed brass legs. They bought an L-shaped sofa upholstered in light grey Belgian linen. They bought a fifty-five-inch OLED television on twelve months of 'No-Cost EMI' through his platinum credit card, followed by a double-door smart refrigerator that sent notifications to Ruchira's phone whenever the humidity in the vegetable crisper dropped below sixty percent.

Next came the car.

In Sector 56, Bhaskar had driven a seven-year-old silver Hyundai hatchback with a dent in the rear bumper from a collision with an auto-rickshaw in Huda City Centre.

On his third morning at *The Pinnacle Crest*, he drove the Hyundai to the basement ramp. The security guard at the barrier glanced at the faded car, hesitated, and tapped on the glass with an iron flashlight, demanding to see his resident RFID sticker before opening the boom barrier.

Behind him, an Audi Q5 and a BMW 3-Series idled with their xenon headlights glaring into his rearview mirror.

Two weeks later, Bhaskar drove home a dark grey German crossover SUV.

The ex-showroom price was thirty-two lakhs. The down payment took every rupee of his annual performance bonus, along with four lakhs liquidated from a mutual fund he had started in his twenties. The monthly EMI was forty-two thousand eight hundred rupees, deducted automatically from his HDFC salary account on the fifth of every month.

Finally, there was Neil.

Their seven-year-old son had been studying at a reputable Christian missionary school near the civil lines, where the fees were eight thousand rupees a month and the children wore navy shorts and carried steel tiffin boxes.

At the society clubhouse, during a Saturday evening pool party, three mothers from Tower B asked Ruchira where Neil studied.

When Ruchira told them, the women had smiled—a tight, pitying compression of glossed lips that lasted precisely one second.

'Oh,' one mother said, adjusting her designer sunglasses. 'Of course. Very traditional. But don't you worry about the child's global exposure? Ayan is at the Cambridge Heritage Academy. They do Finnish experiential pedagogy. They have an indoor heated equestrian ring, and the kids learn computational logic in Grade Two.'

By August, Neil was enrolled at the Cambridge Heritage Academy.

The quarterly admission retainer was one lakh twenty thousand rupees. The annual development levy was seventy-five thousand. The uniform kit—including horse-riding breeches, an embroidered blazer, and a specialized iPad loaded with proprietary learning software—cost thirty-six thousand rupees.

storySections.heading: III. The 2:00 AM Spreadsheet
storySections.body:
The reckoning occurred on the night of October 28th, forty-eight hours before the monthly salary credit.

Bhaskar woke up at 1:45 AM. His throat was dry; his skull felt tight and congested, as if someone had wrapped a thick strip of wet linen around his temples.

He walked into the dark kitchen, poured a glass of cold RO water from the smart refrigerator, and sat down at the smoked-glass dining table.

The apartment was silent. The central ducted air conditioning emitted a faint, low-frequency hum that vibrated through the floorboards like the engine room of an ocean liner. Outside the floor-to-ceiling double-glazed windows, the concrete towers of Golf Course Extension Road rose into the orange smog of the Haryana night, their red aircraft-warning beacons pulsing in unison.

Bhaskar opened his laptop.

He launched Microsoft Excel. He created a new spreadsheet titled *CASH_FLOW_OCTOBER.xlsx*.

For two hours, he logged every recurring liability against their household income. He pulled statements from two credit cards, three loan accounts, and his primary salary ledger.

He lined up the numbers with forensic precision:

*Monthly In-Hand Net Salary:* **₹2,14,000**  
*(After TDS deductions of ₹52,000 and Provident Fund of ₹21,500)*  
*Ruchira's Net Editorial Salary:* **₹62,000**  
**Total Household Monthly Net:** **₹2,76,000**  

Then he listed the debits:

- Apartment Rent: **₹88,000**
- Society Maintenance & Sinking Fund: **₹14,500**
- German SUV Loan EMI: **₹42,800**
- Neil's School Tuition & Bus Transit: **₹48,000**
- Neil's Weekend Tennis & Coding Academy: **₹14,000**
- Full-time Live-in Domestic Helper: **₹18,000**
- Part-time Driver for Ruchira: **₹16,000**
- Electricity Bill (Ducted AC & Geysers): **₹17,200**
- Society Club Minimum Consumption Levy: **₹6,000**
- Organic Grocery Delivery Subscription: **₹24,000**
- High-Speed Fiber & Streaming Services: **₹3,200**
- Credit Card EMI (Sofa & Smart Fridge): **₹18,400**

Bhaskar clicked the *AutoSum* button.

The cell at the bottom of Column B updated instantly with a soft click:

**Total Fixed Monthly Outflow:** **₹3,20,100**

Bhaskar stared at the screen.

He selected the cell. He pressed *F2*. He verified the formula: [=SUM(B4:B15)].

There was no error.

Their fixed monthly expenditure was three lakhs twenty thousand and one hundred rupees.

Their combined monthly in-hand income was two lakhs seventy-six thousand rupees.

Every single month, before they bought a single cup of coffee, before they purchased fuel for the German SUV, before they bought a pair of socks or attended a birthday party, their household was running a net operating deficit of **forty-four thousand one hundred rupees**.

Where was the difference coming from?

Bhaskar opened his secondary credit card statement.

The gap was being swallowed by the revolving balance on his platinum card—a rolling debt of three lakhs eighty thousand rupees, accumulating interest at an annual percentage rate of forty-two percent, masked under the polite, deceptive heading of *Minimum Amount Due: ₹19,200*.

Bhaskar closed his eyes.

A cold, greasy sweat broke out on his neck.

At thirty-six, earning thirty-four and a half lakhs a year—the top one percent of income earners in a country of one point four billion people—he was technically insolvent.

If his quick-commerce company missed its unit-economics target next quarter and laid him off, his family would be evicted from *The Pinnacle Crest* in sixty days. They had zero liquid savings. They had no emergency fund. Their entire net worth consisted of eight lakhs in locked retirement funds, a German car depreciating at twenty percent a year, and eight hundred square feet of Belgian linen and smoked glass that belonged to an HDFC bank loan.

He looked around the magnificent, darkened living room.

The Italian marble floor shone under the ambient orange light of the city. The gold-tinted windows were clean and spotless.

It was not a home. It was a high-velocity extraction chamber designed to capture every single rupee of surplus labor he produced and siphon it directly into the balance sheets of real estate developers, private equity school conglomerates, and European automotive conglomerates.

He put his head down on the smoked glass and listened to the hum of the air conditioner.

storySections.heading: IV. The Father's Janata Watch
storySections.body:
Two weeks later, Bhaskar's father, Tarun Sen, arrived from Durgapur on the Howrah-New Delhi Rajdhani Express.

He arrived carrying a battered blue steel VIP suitcase tied around the middle with a green nylon clothesline to keep the latch from springing open. He wore a faded beige bush shirt, dark terrycotton trousers with two pleats, and a mechanical HMT Janata wristwatch with a scuffed acrylic crystal and a black leather strap that had been repaired twice with superglue.

Bhaskar picked him up from the New Delhi railway station in the German SUV.

As they crossed the toll plaza into Gurgaon, Tarun Sen looked out through the tinted glass at the thirty-story apartment towers lining the Golf Course Road.

'How many people live in these towers, Bhaskar?' the old man asked, adjusting his reading glasses.

'Each society has about eight hundred families, Baba,' Bhaskar said.

'And they all work in computers?'

'Most of them. Technology, finance, consulting.'

When they reached *The Pinnacle Crest*, the security guards saluted the SUV. The electronic barrier lifted with a sharp, mechanical chime. They descended into the subterranean parking garage, where five hundred luxury vehicles sat under bright LED tubes like planes in an underground hangar.

Tarun Sen walked through the marble lobby with slow, hesitant steps, his leather sandals making a loud *slap-slap* sound against the polished floor.

He stayed in the guest bedroom for five days.

He was a quiet, modest guest. Every morning at 5:30, before the ducted AC clicked off, he would wake up, walk into the guest bathroom, and hand-wash his two cotton handkerchiefs and his undershirt in the porcelain sink using a cake of Lifebuoy soap he had brought in his suitcase. He would hang them over the glass shower enclosure to dry.

On the third evening, while Ruchira was on a conference call with an author in London and Neil was doing his computational logic homework on his school iPad, Tarun Sen walked into the kitchen.

Bhaskar was standing by the counter, peeling an orange.

The old man walked over to the floor-to-ceiling glass window. He looked down at the landscaped gardens eighteen floors below—at the Ukrainian tennis instructor coaching a ten-year-old girl under stadium floodlights, at the artificial waterfall tumbling over fake rocks.

'It is very beautiful, Bhaskar,' Tarun Sen said quietly, in his slow, measured Bengali.

'Yes, Baba,' Bhaskar said.

'How much does a flat like this cost to buy?'

'About four and a half crores,' Bhaskar said. 'We are renting it. The rent is eighty-eight thousand.'

Tarun Sen looked at his son.

The old man's face was lined with the quiet, uncorrupted dignity of a man who had never owed a single rupee to any bank in his life. He had built a modest two-story brick house in Durgapur over fourteen years, paying for the bricks as his salary increments came in, sleeping on a folding cot in the unfinished living room to guard the cement bags against thieves.

'Eighty-eight thousand,' Tarun Sen repeated softly. 'Every month?'

'Yes.'

'And the car downstairs?'

'Forty-two thousand on loan.'

Tarun Sen reached down and touched his mechanical watch. The second hand was sweeping across the white dial with a steady, quiet ticking—a mechanical movement manufactured in Bangalore in 1982, requiring no battery, no software update, no monthly subscription.

'You look very tired, Bhaskar,' the old man said gently.

Bhaskar stopped peeling the orange. He looked down at his hands.

'I am earning thirty-four lakhs, Baba,' Bhaskar said, his voice dropping into a whisper so Ruchira would not hear. 'Ten times what you earned. But I cannot sleep at night. I am terrified every day that I will lose my job and we will have nowhere to go.'

Tarun Sen was quiet for a long time. He turned away from the window.

He placed his hand on Bhaskar's shoulder. His palm was calloused, dry, and warm—the hand of a father who had worked with iron sluice gates in the rain so his son would never have to touch grease.

'Wealth is not the size of the water pipe, my boy,' Tarun Sen said softly. 'Wealth is how much water stays in the cistern after the pump stops. If you have thirty-four lakhs coming in and thirty-five lakhs going out, you are not a rich man. You are just an expensive beggar.'

storySections.heading: V. The Society Diwali Gala
storySections.body:
The break came two weeks later, on the night of the annual Diwali gala at *The Pinnacle Crest*.

The central lawn had been transformed into a fairyland of fairy lights, silver marquees, and live food counters. A caterer from South Delhi was serving wood-fired pizzas, sushi rolls, and champagne cocktails to three hundred residents dressed in silk kurtas and designer lehengas.

Bhaskar and Ruchira stood near the mocktail bar.

Around them, a group of four couples from Tower C were discussing winter vacation itineraries.

'We're doing Verbier for skiing this Christmas,' one man said, adjusting the cuffs of his raw-silk kurta. He was a partner at an investment firm in Cyber City. 'The chalet rental is eighteen thousand euros for the week, but the kids need to learn powder skiing early. Otherwise, by the time they reach sixteen, they can't handle the Swiss slopes.'

'We're doing New Zealand,' a woman replied, sipping her prosecco. 'Self-drive campervan. It's thirty lakhs all-in, but the carbon footprint offset program is included in the package.'

Bhaskar looked at the man's shoes. They were Italian leather loafers with silver horsebit buckles.

He looked at Ruchira.

She was wearing a silk saree she had bought on sale four years ago in Kolkata. Her face was pale under her makeup; her eyes had the hollow, glassy stare of a woman who was mentally calculating whether their credit card limit would cover the fifty-thousand-rupee society Diwali gift distribution for the maintenance staff.

Suddenly, Ruchira set her glass down on the high cocktail table.

'Come with me,' she whispered.

She grabbed his hand and pulled him away from the marquee, away from the sushi counter and the Verbier ski stories, down the stone pathway toward the dark, unlit corner of the complex near the service gate.

They stopped beside the tennis court fence.

'I can't do this anymore, Bhaskar,' Ruchira said.

Her voice was not angry. It was flat, exhausted, and completely broken.

'Do what?'

'This,' she said, gesturing toward the glittering towers overhead. 'The rent. The Ukrainian tennis coach. The eighty-rupee organic avocados that rot in the smart fridge. The four-lakh school fees for a seven-year-old child who comes home and asks why we don't have a private elevator like Ayan's family.'

She looked at him, her eyes shining with tears under the distant halogen lamps.

'We are killing ourselves, Bhaskar,' she said. 'You are working fourteen hours a day, screaming at dark-store managers until your blood pressure is one sixty over ninety. I am taking freelance editing projects until 2:00 AM. And for what? So that three women in Tower B think we are respectable?'

Bhaskar looked at her.

He remembered the Excel sheet. He remembered his father's words: *You are just an expensive beggar.*

'What do you want to do?' he asked.

Ruchira took a deep, shuddering breath.

'I want to leave,' she said. 'I want to find a three-bedroom floor in an old sector—Sector 14, or Sector 46. Where the trees are old and the landlord is a retired schoolteacher who drinks tea on the porch. I want to sell the German car and buy a second-hand Maruti. I want to send Neil to a normal school where children play football with plastic balls and nobody knows what a Verbier chalet is.'

She looked up at him, searching his face for resistance.

'Can we do that, Bhaskar? Or will you feel like you have failed?'

Bhaskar looked up at the eighteenth floor of Tower B.

He saw the gold-tinted windows of his apartment—a tiny, illuminated cell suspended in the Gurgaon night sky, purchased with his sanity and held together by four credit cards.

A strange, miraculous laughter rose in his throat.

'No, Ruchi,' he said, pulling her against his chest and burying his face in her hair. 'I won't feel like I have failed. I will feel like I just got out of prison.'

storySections.heading: VI. The Subtraction
storySections.body:
The subtraction took four months to complete.

In January, Bhaskar listed the German SUV on a pre-owned automotive portal. A used-car dealer from Karol Bagh bought it for twenty-four lakhs. The sale proceeds cleared the remaining balance of the car loan and left him with eight hundred and forty thousand rupees, which he immediately used to settle the revolving debt on both platinum credit cards.

He surrendered the cards to the bank, cutting the plastic through the gold microchip with kitchen shears.

In February, they gave three months' notice to the landlord at *The Pinnacle Crest*.

By April, they had moved into the first floor of an independent builder house in Sector 14—an old, quiet residential sector developed by the Haryana government in the 1980s.

The house had terrazzo floors, high ceilings, and a front veranda shaded by two colossal jamun trees whose leaves rustled in the afternoon wind. The rent was thirty-four thousand rupees a month.

Neil was transferred to a local school four hundred meters from their gate. He walked to school every morning in the company of three neighborhood children, carrying a canvas backpack with a water bottle swinging from the strap.

On a Sunday morning in May, Bhaskar woke up at 6:00 AM.

There was no central ducted air conditioning humming in the walls. The ceiling fan turned with a gentle, rhythmic whisper; outside the open balcony door, pigeons were cooing on the jamun branches.

Bhaskar walked down the stairs to the street in his cotton shorts and slippers.

He walked to the corner market behind the post office, where an elderly sweet vendor from Mathura operated a deep iron wok over a coal fire.

Bhaskar ordered three plates of hot dal kachoris served on dried leaf plates with spicy potato curry and pickled green chilies.

Neil and Ruchira joined him ten minutes later. They sat on three blue plastic stools on the pavement, the morning sun warming their arms, eating the hot, flaky bread with their fingers.

Neil had a spot of red chili gravy on his nose; he was laughing about a boy in his new class who had brought a pet chameleon to school in a shoe box.

Bhaskar pulled his phone from his pocket.

The monthly salary from his quick-commerce company had been credited thirty-six hours earlier: two lakhs fourteen thousand rupees.

He looked at his bank application.

The rent was paid: thirty-four thousand.  
The school fee was paid: eleven thousand.  
The groceries were bought: twelve thousand.  

Remaining balance in the checking account: **one lakh forty-two thousand rupees**.

No EMI. No credit card revolving interest. No Ukrainian tennis levy. No foreign chalet competition.

Bhaskar set the phone on the plastic stool.

He looked at his son eating kachoris on the pavement. He looked at Ruchira, whose face had regained the soft, luminous warmth she had had when they were twenty-five.

He leaned back against the brick wall of the post office.

The morning wind blew through the jamun leaves, scattering tiny white blossoms across the pavement.

He was earning thirty-four lakhs a year. But for the first time since he had opened that encrypted PDF in Cyber City, he was not rich on paper.

He was rich in the only way that cannot be taxed, liquidated, or taken away: he owned his own morning, and he did not owe a single soul an explanation.
